passages.t: The baby God told to live
passages.happening:
God tells Ezekiel to confront Jerusalem with her abominations (verse 2). Her origins were in Canaan: ‘Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite’ (verse 3). On the day she was born no one cut her cord, washed her, rubbed her with salt or wrapped her in cloths; she was thrown out into the open field, despised (verses 4-5). Then God passed by and saw her lying in her blood, and he said to her, twice, Live (verse 6).

God raised her. When she was grown, ‘I spread My cloak over you’ and ‘entered into a covenant with you, and you became Mine’ (verse 8). He washed and anointed her and dressed her in fine linen and jewels, and she became a queen. ‘Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty, for it was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The chapter compresses centuries into one life. Jerusalem was a Canaanite city held by the Jebusites until David captured it around 1000 BC. Amorites and Hittites were names for the older peoples of the land; Ezekiel's meaning is that Jerusalem had no noble pedigree. Her rise to queen recalls the splendor of David and Solomon.

Every detail of the opening scene was clear to an ancient reader. Newborns were washed, rubbed with salt and wrapped in cloths. A baby left in a field had been abandoned to die, a practice known in the ancient world, especially for unwanted girls. God's word, Live, is her whole future. Spreading a cloak over someone was a gesture of marriage and protection, the one Ruth asked of Boaz.

The prophets often pictured God's covenant with Israel as a marriage, and idolatry as adultery. Cities were commonly pictured as women, so the image was natural for Ezekiel's first hearers.
passages.later: Ruth asked Boaz, ‘Spread the corner of your garment over me, for you are a kinsman-redeemer’ (Ruth 3:9). God remembered Jerusalem's ‘love as a bride’ in the wilderness (Jeremiah 2:2).
passages.asks: Everything Jerusalem had began with God saying to her, Live. Ask what God has given you that you did not earn. And ask whether you remember where you came from.

passages.happening:
‘But because of your fame, you trusted in your beauty and played the harlot’ (verse 15). Jerusalem took the gifts God gave her and used them for idols and shrines on every street (verses 16-25). Worst of all, she took the sons and daughters she had borne to God and sacrificed them to idols (verses 20-21). ‘And in all your abominations and acts of prostitution, you did not remember the days of your youth’ (verse 22). She made alliances with Egypt, Assyria and Babylon, trusting them instead of God (verses 26-29).

So God will gather her lovers, the nations, against her, and they will strip her of everything and tear down her shrines, as a city is laid waste in war (verses 35-41). The chapter describes that judgment in harsh images, which these notes name and do not repeat. ‘Because you did not remember the days of your youth,’ God will bring her deeds down on her own head (verse 43).
passages.hearers:
The lovers are the great powers Judah's kings turned to instead of trusting God. King Ahaz sent temple silver and gold to the Assyrian king around 734 to 732 BC, and King Hezekiah showed his treasures to envoys from Babylon. The sacrifice of children refers to a practice that Kings and Jeremiah link with the Valley of Ben-hinnom and the god Molech, which Josiah tried to stamp out.

The punishment in verses 35 to 41 matches what happens to a city under siege: walls and shrines torn down, wealth taken, houses burned, people killed. The language is deliberately shocking, crude even by Scripture's own standards. It was aimed at the male elders and leaders who first heard it, casting them as a disgraced wife.
passages.later: King Ahaz sent the silver and gold of the temple to the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:8). Josiah defiled Topheth so that no one could sacrifice a child there (2 Kings 23:10).
passages.hard:
How should a chapter be read that pictures God as a husband who exposes and punishes an unfaithful wife, especially by readers who have suffered abuse?

The difficulty is real and should be named plainly. The chapter uses sexual language and pictures a woman stripped and attacked by a mob, with the husband's jealousy as the reason. Many readers, among them many women and survivors of abuse, hear in it the words and patterns of abusive relationships, and the text has been misused to excuse controlling or violent men.

These verses are a picture of a city and a covenant. The wife is Jerusalem as a people, her lovers are the idols and the nations she trusted, and the punishment describes the sack of the city by those same nations. Interpreters weigh the picture differently. Some stress that it is a metaphor for a city, spoken to a mostly male leadership, describing what invasion would do. Others add that the chapter's frame is grace: it begins with rescue and ends with atonement (verse 63). Some, many feminist and trauma-informed interpreters among them, argue that even as a metaphor it draws on and can reinforce ancient norms that treated women's bodies as the place of shame, and that it must be read critically and with lament. All agree that using this chapter to justify the mistreatment of women is a grave misuse.

So it must be said plainly. This is a prophetic picture of God and a city. It gives no warrant for any man to shame, strip, threaten or harm a wife, or anyone, and no one may use it to say that a woman deserves to be hurt.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Jerusalem's sin began when she trusted her beauty instead of the one who gave it. Ask which of God's gifts you have come to trust more than him. And ask what it would mean to remember the days when you had nothing.

passages.t: Sodom's sin, and an everlasting covenant
passages.happening:
People will quote a proverb about Jerusalem: ‘Like mother, like daughter’ (verse 44). Her sisters are Samaria and Sodom, and she is worse than both (verses 46-52). ‘Now this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy’ (verse 49).

Yet God will restore the fortunes of Sodom and Samaria, and of Jerusalem with them (verse 53). ‘But I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you’ (verse 60). Jerusalem will receive her sisters as daughters, and she will know that he is the LORD, ‘so that when I make atonement for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed’ (verse 63).
passages.hearers:
The key word of the chapter is remember. Jerusalem did not remember the days of her youth (verses 22 and 43). God will remember his covenant made in those days (verse 60). And then Jerusalem will remember, and be silent before his mercy (verse 63).

The comparison with Sodom would have stung. Sodom was the byword for wickedness, and Ezekiel names its sin as pride, plenty and indifference to the poor. Samaria had fallen to Assyria in 722 BC. That God promises to restore even these is a surprise. The chapter that began with a baby left to die ends with atonement.
passages.later: Hosea heard the same promise: ‘So I will betroth you to Me forever’ (Hosea 2:19). Jeremiah promised a new covenant, written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-33).
passages.asks: Sodom's sin was pride, plenty and neglect of the poor. Ask where comfort has made you complacent. And ask what it means that God makes atonement for those who broke his covenant.
